dedupe_keys.name: liquidity effects of the events of september 11 2001 on the us payment system

description: This case study analyses how the 11 September 2001 attacks, by damaging infrastructure in Lower Manhattan, disrupted the US interbank payment system: some banks could not send payments through the Federal Reserve's Fedwire funds service, so others did not receive the funds they expected and faced unexpected liquidity shortages. It was written by James J. McAndrews and Simon M. Potter of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and published in its Economic Policy Review, volume 8 number 2, in November 2002. The authors measure how banks' outgoing payments respond to incoming payments from other banks in normal times and after the attacks, using Fedwire data. The article is available free online on the New York Fed website; the underlying transaction data are confidential. Caveats: it covers a single event in a system that has since changed, and results concern large-value payments only. The study found that the Federal Reserve's large injections of liquidity, first through the discount window and then open market operations, were important in letting banks re-establish their normal coordination of payments. For simulation it documents a real cascading failure in a payment network caused by physical infrastructure damage, useful for calibrating network-flow and resilience models of financial infrastructure. It is related to the ECB TARGET2 liquidity stress test record in this catalogue, which simulates similar shocks.
